sections.h2: How Indiana taxes the profit on a house
sections.html:
Hoosier sellers face no standalone levy on property gains. Profit from a house is folded into ordinary income under the individual adjusted gross income tax. The calculation begins with your federal adjusted gross income (the Section 62 definition) and then runs through Indiana's own additions and subtractions. A taxable gain on your federal return therefore shows up on the state return too.

The state rate is 2.95 percent for 2026, stepping down to 2.90 percent for 2027. One flat rate covers all of your income, gain included.

Counties layer a local income tax over the state rate. Howard County, as one example, sits at 0.0235, or 2.35 percent, for periods starting October 1, 2026. Where you lived on January 1 fixes which county rate applies to you, and counties can adjust rates in January and October. The IT-40 booklet prints each county's current figure.

sections.h2: Who qualifies for the federal exclusion
sections.html:
For most owners, this federal break settles whether any profit ever reaches the Indiana calculation. One seller filing alone can shield up to $250,000 of gain from the sale of a main home. A married couple on a joint return can shield up to $500,000.

You must pass two tests, each looking back across the 5 years that end on your closing date:

  • Ownership: you or your spouse held title for at least 24 months of that window.
  • Use: the house was your home for at least 24 months of that window. On a joint return, each spouse has to pass this test.
  • The two 24-month stretches do not have to overlap.
  • A separate limit: if you claimed the exclusion on a different home sale within the previous two years, you cannot claim it again.

A lender or title company that issues a Form 1099-S triggers a reporting duty, so the sale goes on your return even when every dollar of gain is excluded. If part of the gain is taxable, you will also file Schedule D and Form 8949. Someone on qualified official extended duty may elect to pause the five-year clock for as long as ten years.

sections.h2: Federal rates on gain above the exclusion
sections.html:
A house held for more than a year produces long-term gain, which falls into 0, 15 or 20 percent depending on your taxable income. Anything held a year or less counts as short-term and is taxed like wages. The brackets below are the 2025 figures. They shift every year, so look up the current ones before you file.

Filing status0 percent up to15 percent up to
Single$48,350$533,400
Married filing jointly$96,700$600,050
Head of household$64,750$566,700

Taxable income above the 15 percent range moves to 20 percent. The part of a gain tied to past depreciation (unrecaptured section 1250 gain) tops out at 25 percent. Higher earners can also owe the net investment income tax. If you sell your own home at a loss, the loss cannot be deducted.

sections.h2: Which Indiana adjustments matter to a seller?
sections.html:
Start with the order of operations. First decide how much of the gain the federal exclusion removes. Whatever remains lands in federal adjusted gross income, and only then do Indiana's adjustments apply. Most sellers who qualify for the full exclusion never reach the second step.

The handiest adjustment is a subtraction for property tax paid on a principal residence, capped at $2,500 ($1,250 for separate filers). It appears in the statute alongside subtractions for Social Security benefits and some military income.

The same statute lists additions as well, including state income tax deducted on the federal return and certain bonus depreciation and Section 179 amounts. If you ever depreciated the house as a rental, go through that list line by line with a preparer.

Limits can move between legislative sessions. Read the amount in the current Indiana tax booklet before you count on it.

When an heir sells, the taxable gain is measured from a stepped-up starting value. That usually leaves much less profit on paper than the original owner's purchase price would suggest. Basis equals the fair market value on the date of death, or the value on the alternate valuation date when the estate's personal representative chooses that route.

There is one trap. If you or your spouse handed appreciated property to the decedent within a year of death, the basis reverts to the decedent's adjusted basis from just before death. Hold on to the appraisal or the estate's valuation, because it becomes your cost figure at filing time.

Heirs who sell soon after the death often find the sale price barely above the date-of-death value, which leaves little or no gain to report. Waiting a long time before selling lets gain build on the estate's or the heir's side.

Indiana repealed its inheritance tax, and probate decides who may sign the deed. The estate tax and probate pages on this site cover those steps.

The exclusion is written for a main home, so a rental normally produces taxable gain. The federal side taxes the depreciation-recapture portion at no more than 25 percent.

Indiana then applies its own rate to the federal figure after state modifications. What you owe in total depends on three things: your federal bracket, your county rate and whether any part of the gain qualifies for the exclusion.

Owners of a rental who plan to sell should also decide early whether the tenant stays through closing, since a buyer who wants to move in will price the house differently from one who wants rent.

A tenant in the house adds a second set of questions about notice and timing. The Indiana eviction process page walks through them.

sections.h2: Paperwork to gather before you talk to a preparer
sections.html:
A preparer can give you a useful estimate in one sitting when the records are ready. Pull together:

  • The closing statement from your purchase, plus receipts for capital improvements
  • The dates you moved in and out, so the 24-month tests can be checked
  • Details of any earlier home sale where you took the exclusion
  • The date of death and the valuation, if the house came to you by inheritance
  • Depreciation schedules, if the house was ever rented
  • Your county of residence on January 1

Selling fast for cash does not alter any of this. The tax follows your basis, your years in the home and your January 1 address, so the records count for more than the identity of the buyer. A cash sale also skips lender underwriting, so the stretch between contract and closing can be short. Collect the records before you list, not after.

faqs.q: What does Indiana charge on profit from a home sale?
faqs.a: Profit flows through the state's individual adjusted gross income tax, currently 2.95 percent for 2026 and dropping to 2.90 percent for 2027. Your county then adds a local income tax.

faqs.q: Is gain covered by the federal exclusion taxed by Indiana?
faqs.a: Generally no. The state return begins with federal adjusted gross income, which leaves out gain you excluded. State additions can alter the picture, so a preparer should read your return.

faqs.q: What is the largest gain a seller can exclude?
faqs.a: A seller filing alone can exclude $250,000, and spouses filing together can exclude $500,000. Both need to pass the ownership and residence tests across 24 of the prior 60 months, with no other exclusion claimed in the last two years.

faqs.q: Does an heir owe tax measured from what the owner originally paid?
faqs.a: No, the starting value is the market value on the date of death. A gift of appreciated property to the decedent in the year before death changes that rule.

faqs.q: Must I report a sale that produced no taxable gain?
faqs.a: If a Form 1099-S arrives, yes. Schedule D and Form 8949 enter the picture only when some of the profit is taxable.
